unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8 of your Year 8 English course. This unit is called Global Storytelling and Creativity, and it is one of the most exciting units you will explore this year. Throughout this unit, you will discover how stories shape the world around us, how creative people use language to inspire and persuade, and how you can develop your own storytelling skills. You will read a powerful original story called The Edge of the Infinite, which follows a young storyteller named Imani as she competes in a national youth storytelling competition in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Her journey will show you that great stories do not simply entertain people; they change lives, preserve memories, and give voice to communities that might otherwise be forgotten.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A strong, organised effort to achieve something important for a cause.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The students launched a campaign to raise money for their school library.
practiceSentences: The librarian led a tireless campaign to bring mobile book vans to the distant villages.
How did one letter to a newspaper grow into a national campaign for children's libraries?
"Join our campaign for cleaner beaches," urged the poster in the community centre window.
I would gladly join a campaign to save the town's last cinema from demolition.
The advertising campaign used a single photograph and eleven carefully chosen words.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: c - a - m - p - a - i - g - n
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask the learner to plan a short campaign for a cause they care about, naming its goal and its first action. Their answer should use the word 'campaign' at least twice.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To make something clear or easier to understand.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Can you clarify what you mean by that?
practiceSentences: A good storyteller pauses to clarify who is speaking before the plot races ahead.
Could you clarify whether this legend comes from the coast or from the highlands?
"Let me clarify my point," said the editor, "because the summary blurred two separate ideas."
I asked the poet to clarify her final image, and her answer changed how I read the whole poem.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: c - l - a - r - i - f - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Give me a muddled two-sentence summary of any story and ask me to clarify it, then check I used 'clarify' correctly when I explain my changes.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To attack someone or something violently or with strong words.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The pressure assailed everyone during finals week.
practiceSentences: Doubts began to assail the young author on the night before her book launch.
Why do critics assail every retelling of the epic instead of judging each on its merits?
"Questions will assail you after the screening," warned the director, "so prepare honest answers."
Worries used to assail me before performances until I learned to focus on the first line only.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: a - s - s - a - i - l
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Quiz me on 'assail', then ask me to describe a moment when doubts assailed a performer and how they steadied themselves.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Something that has no limits or end; it goes on forever.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The universe is so big that it seems infinite.
practiceSentences: A skilled narrator can conjure infinite worlds from a handful of ordinary words.
Is the library of possible stories truly infinite, or do all tales share a few ancient roots?
"Children have infinite patience for a good story," smiled the puppeteer, "and none for a dull one."
Staring at the desert sky, I felt the infinite scale of the universe press gently on my imagination.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: i - n - f - i - n - i - t - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to contrast 'infinite' with 'very large', then challenge me to use 'infinite' in a sentence about stories or the sea.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To make someone want to do something or work harder.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The teacher tried to motivate the students by giving them fun projects.
practiceSentences: Folk tales often motivate listeners by showing ordinary people outwitting powerful tyrants.
What could motivate a busy farmer to walk ten miles just to hear a travelling storyteller?
"Deadlines motivate me far more than inspiration does," confessed the novelist during the interview.
Reading about young inventors motivates me to finish my projects instead of merely planning them.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: m - o - t - i - v - a - t - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me what motivates me to finish difficult work, and check that I use 'motivate' or 'motivates' correctly at least twice.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: The ability to keep going and not get tired easily.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: Running every day helped her build her stamina for the marathon.
practiceSentences: Reciting an entire epic from memory demands stamina as well as artistry.
How do the interpreters maintain their stamina during festivals that run late into the night?
"Build your stamina with short daily practices," the drama teacher advised the new cast.
Training for the relay taught me that stamina grows quietly, one unremarkable session at a time.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: s - t - a - m - i - n - a
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to explain the difference between talent and stamina for a storyteller, using 'stamina' in at least two sentences.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Strange or mysterious, often in a way that is unsettling.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She had an uncanny ability to guess what people were thinking.
practiceSentences: The twins share an uncanny ability to finish each other's stories without missing a beat.
Isn't it uncanny how folk tales from distant continents echo the very same warnings?
"Her impression of the headmaster is uncanny," whispered Theo, trying hard not to laugh.
I felt an uncanny sense of recognition in the old city, as if my grandmother's stories had mapped it for me.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: u - n - c - a - n - n - y
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe something uncanny from a story I know, then check my sentence keeps the unsettling sense of the word.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To be full of or to have a lot of something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The garden was teeming with colourful flowers in the spring.
practiceSentences: The bazaar seemed to teem with stories, each stall holder eager to share one.
Why do the world's oldest myths teem with rivers, serpents, and impossible journeys?
"These pages teem with life," wrote the reviewer, "from the first line to the last."
On summer evenings our courtyard would teem with cousins demanding one more chapter.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: t - e - e - m
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe a market or festival using 'teem' or 'teeming', then ask one follow-up question about my description.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Connected to the topic or situation being discussed.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The teacher said our homework was relevant to what we were learning.
practiceSentences: A century later, the fable's warning about greed remains painfully relevant.
How do you keep an ancient legend relevant for listeners raised on video games?
"Cut anything that is not relevant," said the editor, "however beautiful the sentence may be."
I opened my speech with a relevant proverb, and the restless audience settled immediately.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: r - e - l - e - v - a - n - t
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Give me an old proverb and ask me to argue whether it is still relevant today, using 'relevant' at least twice.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Able to be shaped or bent easily without breaking.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The metal is malleable, so it can be formed into different shapes.
practiceSentences: Myths are remarkably malleable, reshaped by every generation that retells them.
Why is memory so malleable that two witnesses can honestly describe different events?
"Keep the clay malleable," said the sculptor, "by wrapping it in a damp cloth overnight."
My plans for the story stayed malleable until the characters began making their own decisions.
dictionaryLinks.spellingPractice: m - a - l - l - e - a - b - l - e
dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to name one literally malleable material and one figuratively malleable thing, such as memory, and check both sentences.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Very eager or enthusiastic about something.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She is an avid reader who finishes a book every week.
practiceSentences: An avid collector of folk tales, Professor Kian filled forty notebooks in a single decade.
What turns a reluctant reader into an avid one: the right book or the right moment?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me what I am an avid reader, watcher or collector of, and check that 'avid' sits before the right noun in my answer.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Taking unnecessary risks without thinking about consequences.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: It was foolhardy of him to climb without safety gear.
practiceSentences: Only a foolhardy sailor ignores the old stories about the reef at low tide.
Was the hero of the legend truly brave, or simply foolhardy with astonishing luck?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to explain the difference between brave and foolhardy, with one example of each from a story or from real life.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To stick out or extend beyond something else.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The rocks jut out from the cliff, making it look dramatic.
practiceSentences: Ancient watchtowers jut from the coastline like sentences left deliberately unfinished.
Why do the rocks jut so dramatically there, as if the island itself were telling a story?
"See how the balconies jut over the alley," said the guide; "storytellers once performed beneath them."

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe a coastline or a city skyline using 'jut', then ask me to add one more detail to sharpen the image.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The dark clouds looked ominous, making us worry about the storm.
practiceSentences: The tale opens with an ominous knock that no character dares to answer.
What makes a single drumbeat feel more ominous than a whole page of description?
"The silence backstage felt ominous," recalled Tia, "until the curtain finally rose."

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to write an ominous opening line for a story, then discuss whether 'ominous' truly describes my line and why.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: Pleasantly warm and comfortable, often describing nice weather.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: We enjoyed a balmy evening at the beach.
practiceSentences: On balmy evenings the whole neighbourhood gathered on the rooftop to trade stories.
Could there be a better setting for poetry than a balmy night beside the sea?
"Enjoy this balmy weather," said the fisherman, "for the monsoon rewrites everything next month."

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to set a scene on a balmy evening in two sentences, and check that 'balmy' describes the weather, not a person.

dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The king issued a decree that everyone must celebrate the festival.
practiceSentences: According to the legend, a royal decree ordered every village to keep one storyteller.
Which decree did the citizens resent more: the tax on salt or the ban on evening gatherings?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to invent a school decree for one week, using 'decree' correctly, then ask who has the authority to issue one.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To move gently through the air, often describing smells or sounds.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The smell of fresh cookies wafted through the kitchen.
practiceSentences: The scent of cardamom coffee would waft through the courtyard as the storyteller cleared his throat.
How does the sound of the bell waft so clearly across the water at dawn?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me to describe three things that can waft — a smell, a sound and something of my choice — in complete sentences.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: To get better after being sick or tired.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: After her illness, she needed a few weeks to recuperate.
practiceSentences: After the exhausting festival tour, the theatre troupe travelled to the coast to recuperate.
How long did the singer need to recuperate before her voice regained its full range?

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me what helps a person recuperate after illness or a long competition, checking I use 'recuperate' at least twice.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A quality or ability that a person is born with, not learned.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: She has an innate talent for music.
practiceSentences: Some scholars argue that storytelling reflects an innate human need to make sense of chaos.

dictionaryLinks.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me whether I think storytelling talent is innate or learned, and make sure I use 'innate' correctly in my argument.

dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: I went to the counter to buy a ticket for the movie.
practiceSentences: The storyteller set up his stool beside the bakery counter, trading tales for warm bread.

dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The clown's antics made everyone at the party laugh.
practiceSentences: The shadow puppets' antics kept even the adults laughing long after midnight.

practiceSentences: The affluent merchant funded a library so that the dock workers' children could study in the evenings.

practiceSentences: Local businesses offered generous support to keep the storytelling festival free for families.

dictionaryLinks.childMeaning: A short and interesting story about a real event or person.
dictionaryLinks.exampleSentence: The teacher shared an anecdote about her first day at school.
practiceSentences: The lecture came alive when the professor shared an anecdote about losing his notes in Cairo.

"Begin with an anecdote," advised the editor, "and the reader will follow you anywhere."

practiceSentences: The novel is set during a scarcity of paper, when letters were written in the margins of old books.

readings.title: Why Stories Shape the World
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Long before printing presses reached the East African coast, stories carried everything a community needed to remember. Somali oral poetry preserved family histories, trade routes and hard-won warnings about drought. Along the Swahili coast, sailors traded tales at harbour counters the way they traded cloth and spice. A story cost nothing to carry, weighed nothing in a boat, and yet it could outlast the ship, the sailor and sometimes the harbour itself.
This unit, Global Storytelling and Creativity, asks you to study that power carefully, and then to use it.
Consider what a story can do that an official report cannot. A government may issue a decree, and people may obey it, but no decree can order anyone to care. A single well-chosen anecdote can carry more truth than a page of statistics, because listeners see themselves inside it. That is why campaigners, teachers, judges and journalists all reach for stories when facts alone fail to move people. A campaign for cleaner water gains force when a grandmother describes the river she swam in as a girl; the same facts in a spreadsheet rarely motivate anyone.
Stories also guard communities against the scarcity of official records. Affluent nations fill archives, museums and libraries with documents, but many communities have carried their history in spoken word alone, passed from elder to child. When a flood, a war or simple neglect destroys the written record, the told story is often the only copy left. Whoever keeps the stories is never a subordinate figure in a community; the storyteller holds the keys to its memory.
Today the tradition is changing shape, not disappearing. Every festival season, the streets of the old harbour quarter teem with poets, drummers and film crews. Young creators mix documentary with fiction, record their grandparents on their phones, and publish in three languages before breakfast. The tools are new; the innate human need to shape experience into narrative is ancient. Scientists who study memory report an uncanny pattern: people forget lists within hours, yet they can retell a story heard once, years later, almost intact.
In this unit you will read The Edge of the Infinite, an original story about Imani, a young storyteller who enters the National Youth StoryForge competition in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Her journey shows that great stories do not simply entertain. They preserve memories, challenge comfortable silences, and give a voice to communities that might otherwise be forgotten.
Along the way you will build a demanding vocabulary, with words such as campaign, anecdote, scarcity, feasible and engross, and you will learn to wield the grammar that professional storytellers depend on, from the present perfect continuous to reported speech. You will practise reading closely, questioning what a text asks you to believe, and checking who is telling the story and why. Those questions matter, because every storyteller makes choices, and every choice shapes what the audience remembers.
Work through each section at your own pace. Revisit anything you find difficult, use your AI tutor whenever you need another explanation, and bring your questions to your twice-weekly meetings with your teacher. By the end of the unit you will plan, draft and polish your own narrative, and you will present a sustained spoken argument about why storytelling still matters.
The support you need is built into every section; the stamina must be your own. Give this unit your full attention and you will finish it with something better than a mark: a voice that other people want to listen to, and the judgement to use it well.

readings.title: The Grammar of a Good Story
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Grammar is the framework that holds a story upright. A storyteller's ideas may be vivid, but without control of tense, voice and word order, the audience receives only a blur. This text walks through the grammar you will master in this unit and shows what each structure is for.
Begin with the unit's main focus, the present perfect continuous. Its structure is simple: subject plus has or have, plus been, plus the verb in its -ing form. Use have been with I, you, we and they, and has been with he, she and it. For the negative, place not after has or have: she has not been sleeping well. For a question, move has or have before the subject: have you been waiting long? The tense connects a past starting point to the present moment, which makes it the natural tense of dedication. The story you are about to read shifts it one step into the past, so you meet lines like Imani had been writing since she was ten, and the effect is the same: you feel the weight of all that invisible effort. Compare she wrote stories with she has been writing stories since she was ten. The first reports a fact; the second opens a window onto years of quiet work.
Reported speech is the narrator's tool. A storyteller cannot pause to quote every character directly, so English provides a way to fold speech into the narration: shift the pronouns, move the tense one step back, and adjust expressions of time and place. "I love this story," she said becomes she said she loved that story. Use said when the listener is not named, and told when the listener is named: he told me he would come. Questions change their word order, so "Are you coming?" becomes she asked if I was coming, and commands take the infinitive: "Please help me" becomes he asked me to help him.
Prepositional phrases pin a scene to a time and place. Small words such as in, at, on, during, for and of connect nouns to the rest of the sentence: at the scene, at the counter, during the campaign, a scarcity of clean water. Choosing the right preposition is a matter of habit rather than logic, and wide reading builds that habit faster than any rule.
The past perfect works alongside the past simple to keep a timeline honest. The past simple reports events in order: the audience clapped. The past perfect steps further back to show what happened first: Imani had already left the stage when the audience clapped. Think of it as the past of the past.
An adjective followed by an infinitive lets a writer pass judgement in a single breath: it is feasible to support the planet; it was foolhardy to ignore the warnings; she was eager to compete. Comparatives and superlatives measure people and claims against each other, so her story was more relevant than most speeches, and the final performance was the most engrossing of the whole competition. Finally, adverbs such as just, already, ever and never sit between has or have and the past participle: they have just recuperated; she has already finished; have you ever performed on a stage? Yet belongs at the end of negatives and questions: I have not finished yet.
None of this is decoration. Choose the tense deliberately, and even a simple sentence about tea can engross a reader. Master these structures one at a time, test them in your own writing, and by the end of the unit they will no longer be rules you remember. They will be instincts you use.

readings.title: The Edge of the Infinite, part 1
readings.theme: Passion, perseverance and the power of storytelling
readings.setting: Dar es Salaam and the Tanzanian coast
readings.passageScript:
Every year, the coastal city of Dar es Salaam teemed with talent, ideas and noise during the National Youth StoryForge. This year, however, the competition was unlike any that had come before.
It was no longer just about performance. For the first time, the Ministry of Public Memory had merged the contest with the National Change Campaign, a new initiative that used stories to spotlight climate, history and hidden voices across Tanzania.
At the Mambo Media Academy, students had been preparing for months. It was a campaign of ideas, a passionate effort to bring forgotten truths to the stage.
For twelve weeks they had trained under mentors, building endurance and style. The stakes were high: the winners would be broadcast on the national grid, and their words would be archived in a cultural capsule for future generations.
Imani, a seventeen-year-old with an avid curiosity and endless stamina, had been writing since she was ten. She kept her stories hidden until one teacher, Mr. Rohan, discovered her notebook of anecdotes and pushed her to audition.
Now she stood at the edge of the outdoor amphitheatre, her heart pounding. Her breath came fast as a balmy ocean breeze rolled through, lifting the scent of roasted maize from the warming plastic chairs.
Inside the preparation tent, the air was thick with commotion: last-minute lines being rehearsed, costumes being adjusted, and an explosion of jargon as students critiqued one another's story arcs.
"You need to clarify the second act!" someone barked.
"Your metaphor's too malleable — what does the fire actually represent?"
Imani kept to herself, sipping ginger tea. She had written a piece called The Flood That Forgot No One, a tale about a girl who learns to speak the ocean's language after her island sinks.
"You're on in three," said a voice. It was Amara, her mentor — sharp-eyed and calm.
Imani swallowed. "What if it's not... relevant enough?"
Amara raised an eyebrow. "You have been campaigning for three months. This story is more relevant than most speeches I have heard in parliament."
That helped. A little.
Out on stage, another performer finished a vivid retelling of a market fire in Mwanza. His voice had wafted across the audience like smoke, leaving them hushed.
Now it was Imani's turn.
She stepped onto the stage. The sea was behind her. Lights framed her. A single microphone waited. Storm clouds gathered far out over the water, ominous, as if the sea itself were listening.
She began: "I have always feared water. Not because it drowns. But because it remembers."
An uncanny stillness settled over the amphitheatre. She pushed forward.
"My grandmother said the sea had an infinite tongue. That it told every story you tried to bury. She told me, when I was five, about the day our island cracked."
As she spoke, Imani's voice grew stronger. She had been polishing the piece for weeks, editing at dawn and rehearsing after lights out. Every word came from her bones.
"I saw boats become coffins. I saw truth jut from the waves like forgotten bones."
Someone at the back gasped.
Imani told of the silence after the flood. Of the scarcity of memory. Of how even officials had denied it.
"'It didn't happen,' they said. But we knew. We had dreams of drowning every night."
She ended with a single line: "And when you deny the past, you abet the next flood."
Silence. Then applause — slow at first, then swelling.
Backstage, Amara pulled her into a hug. "You did it."
"I feel like I have just... returned from a war," Imani said.
Amara grinned. "That is how you know it was real."
The next day the results were posted, and Imani had made it into the final ten.
She walked into the common room, where the other students were buzzing.
"That line about the boats?" said another finalist, Tia. "It engrossed everyone. I stopped breathing."
Someone else muttered, "They'll never let her win, though. Too heavy."
Imani smiled. "Let's see."

readings.title: The Edge of the Infinite, part 2
readings.theme: Passion, perseverance and the power of storytelling
readings.setting: Dar es Salaam and the Tanzanian coast
readings.passageScript:
Finals week was even tougher. The pressure assailed everyone. One student fainted, two others dropped out, and Imani had to recuperate after a night of nausea.
Amara kept her focused. "You have the stamina. Now use it wisely. Speak not just to perform — speak to change."
"Talent may be innate," she added, "but a voice is built, sentence by sentence."
They refined the ending, smoothed the transitions and sharpened every pause. Imani's script now closed with a direct challenge: "What stories will you tell when the waters rise?"
The night of the final broadcast arrived. Lights lit the open-air venue while camera drones hovered above, filming. Ministers sat in the front row, and screens flickered in cafes across the country.
Imani wore a simple white gown. No props. Just her voice.
She began again, slower this time, and louder.
She told the same tale — but fuller. She added moments of humour, antics shared with her cousins before the storm. She described her uncle's foolhardy decision to stay behind.
"He said, 'I have lived by the sea, and I will die by the sea.' And the sea replied, 'Then let me take you.'"
The audience was engrossed.
She ended with the same line: "What stories will you tell when the waters rise?"
Silence. Then a standing ovation.
Backstage, a minister approached her. "That was... necessary," she said. "And brave."
Later, a judge read the results aloud. Imani had won.
A week later, at the post-competition gala, she stood beside Amara on a rooftop. The breeze was soft and balmy.
"You know," said Amara, "when I met you, you seemed unsure. Soft."
"I still feel soft."
"But your voice? That is steel."
Imani looked at the stars. "What do I do now?"
"Now?" Amara said. "You rest. Then you keep going. The campaign is not over. It has simply changed forms."
Weeks passed. Imani began receiving letters from schools, from climate groups, and even one from a remote village council in Zanzibar. They had heard her story. Her performance had motivated schools to start recording clubs of their own. They wanted her to come and speak. To listen. To help them write new stories.
She travelled to places where the ocean bit the land, where houses had vanished into saltwater, and where memory had ebbed with the tide.
At each stop she gathered new voices. She asked the old women to tell their stories and to record their anecdotes into her tablet. She listened to children who explained the floods with drawings.
And at each place she asked the same question: "What will you tell when the waters come again?"
Eventually she returned to Dar es Salaam, but she was not the same girl who had once worried about metaphors and stage fright. She had once stood trembling at the edge of the infinite; now she walked along it, collecting voices.
She was working on a full series: a documentary woven together with narrative. She had partnered with engineers and artists, building stories from both science and soul.
Her project was called Feasible Futures. It aimed to show not just loss but resilience: solutions, and ways forward. Because it was feasible to support the planet, and it was foolish not to.
And Imani, who had once feared that her words might vanish, now knew better. They would waft into corners she had never seen.
They already had.

comprehension.question: Before printing presses reached the coast, what kinds of knowledge did Somali oral poetry preserve, according to Why Stories Shape the World?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It preserved family histories, trade routes and hard-won warnings about drought.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored in the opening paragraph, which lists family histories, trade routes and drought warnings.

comprehension.question: Which tense does The Grammar of a Good Story call the natural tense of dedication, and what is its structure?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The present perfect continuous, formed with the subject plus has or have, plus been, plus the verb in its -ing form.
comprehension.explanation: Checks the learner can locate the tense of dedication and its has or have plus been plus -ing structure in the second paragraph.

comprehension.question: What is the title of Imani's competition piece, and what is it about?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is called The Flood That Forgot No One, a tale about a girl who learns to speak the ocean's language after her island sinks.
comprehension.explanation: A literal question anchored in the preparation-tent scene of part 1, where the piece and its island tale are named.

comprehension.question: What is Imani's new project called at the end of the story, and what does it aim to show?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is called Feasible Futures, and it aims to show not just loss but resilience, solutions and ways forward.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question from the closing paragraphs of part 2, where the series and its aims are described.

comprehension.question: According to Why Stories Shape the World, why does a story often succeed where a decree or a spreadsheet fails?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A decree can force obedience but cannot order anyone to care, and facts in a spreadsheet rarely motivate; a story lets listeners see themselves inside it, as when a grandmother describes the river she swam in as a girl.
comprehension.explanation: An evidence question: the learner must contrast the decree and the spreadsheet with the grandmother anecdote in paragraph three.

comprehension.question: Why does The Grammar of a Good Story call reported speech the narrator's tool, and what example does it give?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because a storyteller cannot pause to quote every character directly, reported speech folds speech into the narration; the passage turns "I love this story," she said into she said she loved that story.
comprehension.explanation: Tests whether the learner can connect the narrator's-tool claim to the she-said-she-loved-that-story example.

comprehension.question: When Imani worries that her story is not relevant enough, how does Amara answer her, and what does the answer reveal?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amara says Imani has been campaigning for three months and that the story is more relevant than most speeches she has heard in parliament, showing complete confidence in the piece.
comprehension.explanation: An inference-with-evidence question about Amara's parliament remark backstage and what it shows about her belief in Imani.

comprehension.question: What foolhardy decision does Imani's uncle make in her retelling, and how does the sea answer him?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He decides to stay behind, saying he has lived by the sea and will die by the sea, and the sea replies, "Then let me take you."
comprehension.explanation: Anchored in the uncle's dialogue during the final broadcast; the learner must give both halves of the exchange.

comprehension.question: Why does Why Stories Shape the World insist the storyteller is never a subordinate figure in a community without written archives?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because such communities carry their history in spoken word alone, the told story may be the only copy left after a flood, a war or neglect, so the storyteller holds the keys to the community's memory.
comprehension.explanation: A synthesis question linking spoken-word archives, the loss of written records and the storyteller's standing.

comprehension.question: How does the past perfect keep a timeline honest, according to The Grammar of a Good Story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It steps further back than the past simple to show which event happened first, as in Imani had already left the stage when the audience clapped.
comprehension.explanation: An evaluation question about the honest-timeline claim, answered with the had-already-left-the-stage example.

comprehension.question: Imani ends her first performance with "when you deny the past, you abet the next flood." What does she mean, given what the officials said?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The officials denied that the flood ever happened, so Imani means that refusing to admit a disaster helps cause the next one, because nothing is learned and nothing changes.
comprehension.explanation: Requires interpreting the abet line against the officials' denial: denial prevents learning, so it assists the next disaster.

comprehension.question: By the end of the story, what has the title The Edge of the Infinite come to mean for Imani?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She once stood trembling at the edge of the infinite, fearing the sea's memory, but the edge becomes a starting point: she walks along it collecting voices, and her words waft into corners she has never seen.
comprehension.explanation: An interpretation of the title using the epilogue, where the edge turns from a place of fear into a starting point.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Continuous
grammar.explanation: The present perfect continuous describes an action that began in the past and is still continuing now, or has just stopped with visible results, using has or have plus been plus the verb's -ing form.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + has/have + been + verb-ing.
Use have been with I, you, we and they: I have been studying all morning.
Use has been with he, she and it: She has been reading since breakfast.
Negative — add not after has or have: She has not been studying.
Question — move has or have before the subject: Have you been eating well?
Step by step: identify the subject; choose has or have; add been, which is never dropped; add the -ing form of the main verb; finish with a time expression such as since, for, all day or all week.
Examples: They have been working on the project since Monday. I have been learning English for three years. We have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes. She has been writing since she was ten years old. The streets have been teeming with visitors since the festival started. They have been preparing for the competition for three months.
grammar.commonMistake: Three slips break this tense: dropping been (she has working hard), pairing the wrong helper (they has been playing), and forgetting the -ing (I have been play). Keep all three parts in place: they have been playing.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the tense as a bridge: has or have stands on the past bank, been is the span, and the -ing verb walks across into the present moment.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the present perfect continuous: 1) She (dance) ______ for two hours. 2) They (watch) ______ that film since last night. 3) I (read) ______ this book all week. 4) He (train) ______ for the marathon for months. 5) We (wait) ______ for you since morning. 6) The wind (blow) ______ strongly all afternoon. 7) You (practise) ______ your speech for days. 8) It (rain) ______ since we arrived.
Part B — do the same with sentences from the unit's world: 9) She (write) ______ stories since she was a child. 10) They (prepare) ______ for the competition for three months. 11) He (practise) ______ his lines every evening after school. 12) The city (teem) ______ with visitors since the festival began. 13) She (recuperate) ______ at home since her illness last month.
Part C — write two true sentences about your own week in this tense, then check that each keeps has or have, been and the -ing form.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) has been dancing 2) have been watching 3) have been reading 4) has been training 5) have been waiting 6) has been blowing 7) have been practising 8) has been raining.
Part B: 9) has been writing 10) have been preparing 11) has been practising 12) has been teeming 13) has been recuperating.
Part C is open-ended (your own true sentences about your week), so there is no single fixed answer. Self-check instead that each sentence keeps all three parts of the form together: has/have, been, and the -ing form, for example, "I have been reading a new book this week" or "We have been rehearsing our play since Monday."

grammar.title: Reported Speech: Statements, Questions and Commands
grammar.explanation: Reported speech retells what someone said without quoting the exact words, shifting the pronouns, moving the tense one step back, and adjusting expressions of time and place.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Three changes turn direct speech into reported speech.
1) Change the pronouns to fit the new speaker: "I am happy" becomes he said he was happy.
2) Shift the tense one step back: present simple becomes past simple, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, will becomes would, and can becomes could.
3) Adjust time and place words: today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there, and this becomes that.
Said or told: use said when the listener is not named (he said he would come) and told when the listener is named (he told me he would come).
Questions: yes/no questions take if or whether with statement word order — "Are you coming?" becomes she asked if I was coming. Wh-questions keep the question word: "Where are you going?" becomes she asked where I was going.
Commands and requests take to + infinitive: "Please help me" becomes he asked me to help him, and "Don't be late" becomes she told me not to be late.
Examples from the unit: Imani said she had always feared water. Amara told her that the campaign was not over. She asked them to clarify their roles.
grammar.commonMistake: Keeping the original tense (she said she loves reading instead of she said she loved reading) or leaving the quotation marks in place; reported speech folds the words into your own sentence, so no quotation marks remain.
grammar.memoryTip: You are telling the story of a conversation, so shift everything to your own point of view: your pronouns, your tense, your here and your now.
grammar.practice:
Part A — turn each sentence into reported speech: 1) "I love reading," he said. 2) "Can you help me?" she asked. 3) "Please close the door," he requested. 4) "We have been practising all day," they said. 5) "I will finish my story tonight," Imani said. 6) "Where is the competition?" he asked.
Part B — now report these lines from the unit: 7) "Can you clarify the instructions?" she asked. 8) "Please support our campaign," he requested. 9) "The competition will begin tomorrow," the organiser announced. 10) "I had never seen such an engrossing performance," the judge admitted.
Part C — say one sentence aloud to a partner or your AI tutor and have them report it back to you, then swap roles and keep the exchange going for five turns.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) He said (that) he loved reading. 2) She asked if/whether I could help her. 3) He asked/requested me to close the door. 4) They said (that) they had been practising all day. 5) Imani said (that) she would finish her story that night. 6) He asked where the competition was.
Part B: 7) She asked if/whether I could clarify the instructions. 8) He asked/requested me to support their campaign. 9) The organiser announced (that) the competition would begin the next day. 10) The judge admitted (that) they had never seen such an engrossing performance (the past perfect in the original quote is already the furthest-back tense, so it does not shift again).
Part C is an open speaking exchange with no fixed answer. Self-check that every report you make keeps the three changes from the rule: the pronoun shifts to fit the new speaker, the tense steps one back (or stays if it is already the furthest-back tense), and time/place words such as today or here shift to that day or there, with no quotation marks left in the reported version.

grammar.title: Prepositions with Nouns
grammar.explanation: Prepositions such as in, at, on, during, for and of link nouns to the rest of the sentence, building phrases that tell the reader where, when or how something happens.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A prepositional phrase is a preposition plus a noun phrase: at the counter, in the hallway, during the campaign, a scarcity of clean water.
Place: use in for enclosed spaces (in the hallway, in the village), at for points and posts (at the scene, at the counter, at the edge of the stage) and on for surfaces (on the stage, on the coast).
Time: use during for something that happens inside a longer event (during the campaign, during finals week) and for with lengths of time (for three months).
Belonging and amount: of ties a quantity or lack to its noun — a scarcity of water, an explosion of jargon.
Examples: The police arrived at the scene quickly. She waited at the counter to collect her badge. Many people joined during the campaign for cleaner beaches. There was a scarcity of resources in the village. The performers stood at the edge of the stage.
English pairs many nouns with fixed prepositions, so collect the pairings as you read rather than guessing them from logic.
grammar.commonMistake: Swapping the pairings — in the scene instead of at the scene, or on the counter when you mean waiting at the counter — and leaving a phrase unfinished; every preposition needs its noun to complete the picture.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask the sentence two questions, where and when; the answers almost always begin with a preposition, and the noun that follows completes the picture.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with in, at, on, during, for or of: 1) There was a commotion ______ the hallway when the results were announced. 2) The performers waited nervously ______ the counter to collect their badges. 3) The scarcity ______ clean water affected everyone ______ the village. 4) She joined the campaign ______ climate awareness ______ her second year. 5) He stood ______ the edge of the stage, looking out over the sea.
Part B — write three sentences about the story: one saying where Imani performed, one saying when the students trained, and one using a scarcity of. Underline each prepositional phrase you build.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) in (a commotion in the hallway) 2) at (waited at the counter) 3) of ... in (a scarcity of clean water affected everyone in the village) 4) for ... during (joined the campaign for climate awareness during her second year) 5) at (stood at the edge of the stage).
Part B is an open writing task, but the specific story facts it asks for are not printed in this practice field itself, so rather than guessing, check your three sentences against the unit's own reading passages. For where Imani performed, the story says "Now she stood at the edge of the outdoor amphitheatre" and "She stepped onto the stage" — a correct sentence keeps a place preposition such as at or on before the stage or amphitheatre, e.g. "Imani performed on the stage of the outdoor amphitheatre." For when the students trained, the story says "For twelve weeks they had trained under mentors" — a correct sentence keeps for before the length of time, e.g. "The students trained for twelve weeks before the competition." For a scarcity of, follow this item's own examples ("a scarcity of clean water", "a scarcity of resources") and keep of directly after scarcity, followed by the noun that is lacking, e.g. "There was a scarcity of rehearsal time before the show." Underline the preposition-plus-noun phrase in each sentence to confirm it is complete.

grammar.title: Past Perfect vs Past Simple
grammar.explanation: The past simple reports completed events in order, while the past perfect, formed with had plus a past participle, reaches further back to show which event happened first.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Past simple: subject + past form — she finished her homework; the audience clapped.
Past perfect: subject + had + past participle — she had finished her homework before dinner.
Use them together to keep a timeline honest: After she had finished her script, she went home. By the time Imani arrived, the audience had already settled. I saw the film after my friend had recommended it.
Signal words: after, before, by the time and already often mark the earlier action.
When only one past event is mentioned, the past simple alone is enough; reach for the past perfect only when you need to step behind another past event.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting the past perfect on the later action, as in I ate lunch before I had gone to the store; the earlier action takes had, so say I had eaten lunch before I went to the store.
grammar.memoryTip: Draw two timelines: the lower one carries the main past events in the past simple, and anything on the higher, earlier line takes had plus the past participle.
grammar.practice:
Part A — choose the past perfect or the past simple: 1) After they (finish) ______ their homework, they went outside to play. 2) By the time I arrived, the film (start) ______. 3) She (never / see) ______ a lion before her trip to the zoo. 4) He (eat) ______ breakfast before he (leave) ______ for school. 5) The concert (begin) ______ before we (arrive) ______.
Part B — now work with events from the story: 6) By the time the judge (arrive) ______, Imani (already / finish) ______ her performance. 7) She (write) ______ the story before she (enter) ______ the competition. 8) The audience (clap) ______ because they (never / hear) ______ anything so moving. 9) After he (recuperate) ______, he (return) ______ to school. 10) They (leave) ______ the venue after the results (be announced) ______.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) had finished 2) had started 3) had never seen 4) had eaten ... left 5) had begun ... arrived.
Part B: 6) arrived ... had already finished 7) had written ... entered 8) clapped ... had never heard 9) had recuperated ... returned 10) left ... had been announced. (For item 10, "were announced" is also acceptable since "after" alone can sequence the two events, but "had been announced" follows the same pattern as the rule's own worked example, After she had finished her script, she went home, where the earlier action in the after-clause takes the past perfect.)

grammar.title: Adjective + Infinitive
grammar.explanation: An adjective followed by to and a base verb passes judgement on an action in a single phrase, saying what is possible, wise, difficult or exciting to do.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: it is / it was + adjective + to + base verb, or subject + be + adjective + to + base verb.
Choose an adjective that judges the action: feasible, foolhardy, important, difficult, eager, brave, exciting.
Examples: It is feasible to support the plan. It was foolhardy to ignore the warning signs. It is important to listen carefully in class. She is eager to compete in the national finals. It was brave to speak the truth on stage. It is difficult to finish a novel in one day, but not impossible.
The infinitive always keeps its base form; the tense lives in the verb be, so shift is to was to move the judgement into the past.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping to (it's easy eat) or using the -ing form after the adjective (it's important studying); the pattern always takes to plus the base verb: it is easy to eat, and it is important to study.
grammar.memoryTip: Adjective first, then to, then the action: judge first, act second, and let the little word to hinge the two halves together.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the infinitive: 1) It is exciting ______ (go) to the amusement park. 2) It was silly ______ (forget) my homework. 3) It is important ______ (listen) carefully in class. 4) She was happy ______ (win) the competition. 5) It would be foolhardy ______ (ignore) the warning signs.
Part B — complete each sentence with an adjective from the box (feasible, foolhardy, eager, difficult, important) and the infinitive: 6) It is ______ to ______ (support) the environment whenever you can. 7) She was ______ to ______ (compete) in the national finals. 8) It would be ______ to ______ (abet) someone doing something wrong. 9) It is ______ to ______ (finish) a novel in one day, but not impossible. 10) It was ______ to ______ (complete) the project on time once we all worked together.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) to go 2) to forget 3) to listen 4) to win 5) to ignore.
Part B: 6) feasible to support 7) eager to compete 8) foolhardy to abet 9) difficult to finish 10) important to complete.

grammar.title: Comparatives, Superlatives and Adverb Placement
grammar.explanation: Comparatives weigh two things against each other, superlatives crown the extreme among three or more, and adverbs such as just, already, ever and never take a fixed seat inside the present perfect.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparatives: add -er to one-syllable adjectives (taller), change -y to -ier (happier), and use more before longer adjectives (more relevant, more powerful).
Superlatives: add -est (tallest), change -y to -iest (happiest), or use most before longer adjectives (most engrossing).
Irregular forms: good becomes better and best; bad becomes worse and worst.
From the story: Imani's story was more powerful than any speech the judges had heard, and the final broadcast was the most engrossing performance of the competition.
Adverb placement in the present perfect: just, already, ever and never sit between has or have and the past participle — they have just recuperated; she has already finished her piece; have you ever performed outdoors; I have never seen such a talented performer.
Yet stands at the end of negatives and questions: I have not finished yet. Have you finished yet?
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling the comparison (more taller, most fastest) and parking the adverb at the end (they have recuperated just); one comparison marker is enough, and the adverb belongs before the past participle.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the rhyme -er is for two, -est is for a crew, then seat your adverb between the helper and the action like a passenger between two drivers.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the comparative or superlative form: 1) My cat is ______ (soft) than my dog. 2) This is the ______ (exciting) game I have ever played. 3) Your backpack is ______ (heavy) than mine. 4) That was the ______ (funny) film I have seen this year. 5) This story is ______ (relevant) than the last one. 6) The second act was ______ (good) than the first. 7) The weather today is ______ (balmy) than it was yesterday.
Part B — rewrite each sentence with the adverb in the correct position: 8) She has finished her story. (already) 9) Have you tried writing poetry? (ever) 10) They have recovered from the competition. (just) 11) I have seen such a talented performer. (never)
Part C — the mixed challenge: write one present perfect continuous sentence about something you have been doing this week; report this line in reported speech: "The storytelling competition has been inspiring," said the teacher; write one sentence using the past perfect and the past simple together to describe two events from the story; write one sentence with feasible plus an infinitive; and write one comparative sentence about two characters or places from The Edge of the Infinite.

Answer Key:
Part A: 1) softer 2) most exciting 3) heavier 4) funniest 5) more relevant 6) better 7) balmier.
Part B: 8) She has already finished her story. 9) Have you ever tried writing poetry? 10) They have just recovered from the competition. 11) I have never seen such a talented performer.
Part C is a mixed challenge. One line has a fixed answer: reporting "The storytelling competition has been inspiring," said the teacher becomes The teacher said (that) the storytelling competition had been inspiring. The other four tasks are open composition, so self-check them against model examples instead of a fixed answer: present perfect continuous about your week, e.g. "I have been rehearsing my lines every evening this week"; past perfect with past simple about two events from the story, e.g. "By the time the audience clapped, Imani had already stepped off the stage" (matching the rule's own example, Imani had already left the stage when the audience clapped); feasible plus an infinitive, e.g. "It was feasible to finish the script before the deadline"; and a comparative about two characters or places from the story, e.g. "The outdoor amphitheatre felt more thrilling than the preparation tent."

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Story Retelling
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
After reading The Edge of the Infinite, practise retelling the story in your own words. You do not need to memorise every detail; focus on the main events and try to use at least ten vocabulary words from this unit as you speak. You can practise alone by recording yourself, or you can tell the story to a family member, a friend or your AI tutor.
When retelling the story, reach for perfect continuous forms where they fit: instead of saying Imani prepared for months, say Imani had been preparing for months. That one change carries the weight of her effort into your retelling.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Reported Speech Conversations
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with a partner or your AI tutor. One person makes a statement, and the other person reports it. Keep going back and forth, practising the tense shifts and pronoun changes required for reported speech.
Example exchange:
Person A: I have been studying all morning.
Person B reports: She said she had been studying all morning.
Person B: I am excited about the storytelling competition.
Person A reports: He said he was excited about the storytelling competition.
Try to keep the conversation going for at least five minutes. The more you practise, the more natural reported speech will become.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: My Storytelling Campaign

Organise the speech in five moves. Introduction: name your campaign and say why you care. Background: explain how you became interested and what motivated you. Actions: describe what you have been doing to support the cause. Impact: share any results you have noticed. Call to action: invite your audience to join or support the campaign.

quizzes.question: What does 'campaign' mean?
quizzes.options: The ability to keep going and not get tired easily. | A planned series of actions carried out over time to achieve an important goal. | Special words or expressions used by a particular group. | Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A planned series of actions carried out over time to achieve an important goal.
quizzes.explanation: A campaign is a planned, organised effort for a cause, like the students' campaign to raise money for their school library.

quizzes.question: What does 'clarify' mean?
quizzes.options: To stick out or extend beyond something else. | To help someone do something wrong or illegal. | To move gently through the air, often describing smells or sounds. | To make something clear or easier to understand.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To make something clear or easier to understand.
quizzes.explanation: To clarify is to make an idea clearer for your listener, as in: can you clarify what you mean by that?

quizzes.question: What does 'assail' mean?
quizzes.options: To attack someone or something violently or with strong words. | To completely focus on something and not notice anything else. | To make someone want to do something or work harder. | To be full of or to have a lot of something.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To attack someone or something violently or with strong words.
quizzes.explanation: Pressure, doubts or critics can assail a person; the word means to attack with force or with strong words.

quizzes.question: What does 'infinite' mean?
quizzes.options: Strange or mysterious, often in a way that is unsettling. | Pleasantly warm and comfortable, often describing nice weather. | Something that has no limits or end; it goes on forever. | Having a lot of money and wealth.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Something that has no limits or end; it goes on forever.
quizzes.explanation: Infinite describes something without limits or end, like the seemingly infinite universe.
